name: Luhu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: Australian National University. (ANU Pacific Linguistics open-access scan; author's own 1977-79 fieldnotes on Luhu and Piru)
catalog_locator: Ch. V 'Proto-West Piru Bay', sec. 4 'Subgrouping of WPB, Part III: Luhu, Asilulu, Wakasihu and Batumerah', subsection 'Asilulu and Hoamoal' (pp.81ff.): stress statement p.82, with the 'obligatory penultimate stress rule' sentence at the foot of the same page; Piru = Luhu identity statement p.79 (subsection 'Luhu and Hoamoal'); endnotes 116-117 in the Notes section
catalog_quote: [p.82] An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress. For example, [moon / kind of fruit / tomorrow] Asilulu húlan e, ʔúlul e, ráwa e; Luhu huláne, ulúle, rawáʔe. Note too Asilulu palaʔekni [paláʔekən] recall him and Luhu palaʔeʔena [palaʔeʔéna]. ... This obligatory penultimate stress rule not only sometimes obscures cognate reflexes but in a few cases seems to be the motivating force for certain vowel deletions in the antepenultimate syllable. [p.79] If one compares Luhu and Piru, one notices no significant sound differences.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress. For example, [moon / kind of fruit / tomorrow] Asilulu húlan e, ?úlul e, ráwa e; Luhu huláne, ulúle, rawá?e. Note too Asilulu pala?ekni [palá?ekən] recall him and Luhu pala?e?ena [pala?e?éna]. [...] This obligatory penultimate stress rule not only sometimes obscures cognate reflexes but in a few cases seems to be the motivating force for certain vowel deletions in the antepenultimate syllable.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (178 pp.82) at 130 dpi and read the page scan, plus the text of pp.90-93. The quoted sentences are on printed p.82 exactly as reported: "An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress. For example," followed by the table (moon / kind of fruit / tomorrow): Asilulu(fn116) húlan e, ʔúlul e, ráwa e; Luhu huláne, ulúle, rawáʔe; then "Note too Asilulu palaʔekni [paláʔekən] recall him and Lu…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the whole word, including any suffix or (petrified) post-particle: when -e / -ne / -na etc. is added, stress moves right to stay penultimate (huláne, rawá?e, pala?e?éna). This is stated for all Hoamoal languages and exemplified with Luhu forms bearing acute accents; it contrasts with Asilulu, where stress stays on the root penult.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the rule is called 'obligatory' and is said to drive deletion of antepenultimate vowels in some words (kallana 'wave', sumbeke 'shove', mandae 'male', p.83).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; the statement is in a comparative-historical monograph, illustrated with suffixed vs unsuffixed word forms (nouns with the permanent -e suffix, a verb with object suffix). The rule is phrased for the Hoamoal subgroup as a whole (Luhu, Manipa, Kelang, Boano, Wakasihu), with Luhu as the illustrated language; Luhu is the author's own field language (informants incl. Hj. Abd. Rahman Payapo, p.136).
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is made for the Hoamoal subgroup of West Piru Bay (Luhu, Manipa mani1297, Kelang kela1256, Boano boan1242, Wakasihu waka1277) and exemplified with Luhu proper (the Luhu village variety, luhu1243); Piru (piru1241, bookkeeping) is treated by Collins (p.81) and the Holle list as a dialect of Luhu. The same p.82 sentence has already been used in this compilation for boan1242; for Luhu it is first-hand (Collins's own field data with stress-marked Luhu forms), not second-order.

new_statements.quote: The language has further innovated by permanently affixing a demonstrative, -ne ('this'), to the independent pronominal series; furthermore, articles, -e and -a, are suffixed to many nouns, with no productive alternation. This fossilization of some morphological processes has resulted in new stress patterns as well. This permanent shift in stress is probably related to the sporadic occurrence of vowel deletion in the antepenultimate syllable which has created consonant clusters and geminate consonants; for example, **kalúlan-a > kalulána > kallána 'wave'.
new_statements.citation: Collins, James T. 1982. Linguistic Research in Maluku: A Report of Recent Field Work. Oceanic Linguistics 21(1/2): 73-146, esp. pp. 122-123 (Teor-Kur).
new_statements.locator: Section 3.1.7 'Hoamoal', printed pp. 96-97 (PDF pages 24-25 of the 74-page ProQuest scan); page scan read directly for the accent marks
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 74 pages, no text). Rendered PDF pages 24-25 (printed pp. 96-97, section 3.1.7 'Hoamoal') at 200 dpi and read the page scan: the quoted passage from 'The language has further innovated by permanently affixing a demonstrative, -ne ("this"), to the independent pronominal series; furthermore, articles, -e and -a, are suffixed to many nouns, with no productive alternation. This fossilization of some morphological processes has resulted in new stress patterns as well. This permanent shift in stress is probably related to the sporadic occurrence of vowel deletion in the antepenultimate syllable which has created consonant clusters and geminate consonants; for example, **kalúlan-a > kalulána > kal…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate) and as Collins 1983 p. 82, and it adds the mechanism: the fossilized articles -e/-a and demonstrative -ne shifted stress to the new word penult (a 'permanent shift in stress'), which in turn drives antepenultimate vowel deletion (kalulána > kallána) - the same link Collins 1983 makes with its 'obligatory penultimate stress rule.. motivating force for certain vowel deletions in the antepenultimate syllable'. Placement is shown by the accented example rather than stated as a rule, hence medium confidence. Identity: Luhu village on the Hoamoal peninsula; p. 97 'it can be demonstrated that Piru is a dialect of Luhu', i.e. Glottolog luhu1243 Luhu-Piru.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The survey paragraph does not state a placement rule in words; the accented example shows it: after the article -a fused to the noun, stress sits on the penultimate syllable of the whole word (kalulána, kallána), having moved off the old root penult (**kalúlan-a). The resulting unstressed antepenultimate vowel is sporadically deleted, giving clusters and geminates. Read together with Collins 1983 (already in the catalog) this is the penultimate rule counting fossilized suffixes.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress; the vowel deletion in the antepenult is described as 'sporadic'. The paper is a fieldwork survey with no phonology section; only the single Hoamoal paragraph (pp. 96-97) mentions Luhu stress. The 'esp. pp. 122-123 (Teor-Kur)' in the target citation belongs to another language's item (section 3.3.3 Teor and Kur), not to Luhu.
new_statements.identity_note: Collins 1982 describes the language of Luhu village (Hoamoal peninsula, west Seram, >5000 residents) and states (p. 97) that Piru, spoken by a few elderly at the head of Piru Bay, is a dialect of Luhu, close to extinction, with loans via Eti (Kaibobo) - this matches Glottolog luhu1243 Luhu-Piru (lcq). The stress remark concerns Luhu proper; nothing is said about stress in the Piru dialect.

tone.quote: Deskripsi fonologi bahasa Hitu dan bahasa Luhu yang akan diuraikan berikut menyangkut fonem vokal dan konsonan kedua bahasa tersebut. [...] Bahasa Luhu (BL) mengenal enam belas buah fonem segmental, yang terdiri atas lima buah fonem vokal, yaitu /a/, /i/, /u/, /e/, /o/ dan sebelas fonem konsonan, yaitu /p/, /m/, /w/, /t/, /r/, /s/, /l/, /n/, /~n/, /k/, dan /h/. Berikut uraian mengenai fonem vokal dan fonem konsonan BL.
tone.locator: sec. 3.1 'Deskripsi Fonologi Bahasa Hitu dan Bahasa Luhu', p. 21, and sec. 3.1.2 'Fonologi Bahasa Luhu', p. 32
tone.translation: The phonological description of Hitu and Luhu set out below concerns the vowel and consonant phonemes of the two languages. [...] Luhu (BL) has sixteen segmental phonemes, consisting of five vowel phonemes, /a i u e o/, and eleven consonant phonemes, /p m w t r s l n ñ k h/. A description of the vowel and consonant phonemes of BL follows.
